title_ar: الذي يصل للميت و الذي لا يصله
title_en: What Reaches the Dead and What Does Not
body_ar:
ما يعرف عندنا بالتوفية للأموات أي قراءة سورة الإخلاص إحدى عشرة مرة ليلة الجمعة و إرسال ثوابها للأموات هل يصل إليهم؟و هل هو ثابت في السنة أم لا؟

هذا لم يرد في السنة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم و من المعلوم أن الخير هو ما جاء به النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم من عند الله و أن ما لم يأت به لا خير فيه و قراءة القرآن و إهداء ثوابه للأموات محل خلاف بين أهل العلم فمذهب مالك و الشافعي أنه لا يصل و الغريب أن أهل هذه البلاد مالكيون و مع ذلك نجد هذه العادة منتشرة فيهم و مذهب مالك أنه لا يصل مذهب مالك أن القرآءة لا تصل الأموات والذي يصل هو الدعاء و الصدقة و قد قال مولود رحمه الله: أجر الطعام و الدعا إن بذلا للميت لا خلاف في أن يصلا

و مع ذلك مذهب أبي حنيفة و ابن حنبل أن قراءة القرآن و إهداء ثوابه للميت إذا كان الإهداء سابقا على القراءة فإنه يصل قياسا على الصدقة و الدعاء و هذا الذي يسمى بالتلحيق عندهم و هو أن يقول الإنسان قبل قراءته اللهم اجعل ثواب ما سأقرأ و بركة ما سأتلو هدية مني نازلة و رحمة منك واصلة إلى فلان و يذكره فيكون هذا إهداء لذلك العمل إليه

و الحنابلة و الحنفية قاسوا هذا على الحج و العمرة فقد أذن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بالحج و العمرة عن الأموات فقد أخرج البخاري في الصحيح من حديث أنس بن مالك رضي الله عنه أن رجلا من الأنصار أتى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال: إن أمي ماتت و لم تحج أفأحج عنها ؟ قال: حج عن أمك و في رواية حج عن أمك و اعتمر و هي لأبي داوود في السنن و كذلك في حديث الخثعمية أنها قالت: يارسول الله : إن فريضة الله بالحج أدركت أبي شيخا كبيرا لا يمسك نفسه على الرحل أفأحج عنه قال: أرايت لو كان على أبيك دين أكنت قاضيته قالت نعم قال: فأدوا الذي عليه فدين الله أحق بالوفاء و سمع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم رجلا يقول: لبيك اللهم عن شبرمة فقال: أحججت عن نفسك قال: لا قال:فاحجج عن نفسك ثم عن شبرمة و سمع آخر يقول لبيك اللهم عن عرفطة فقال: أحججت عن نفسك قال: لا قال: فاحجج عن نفسك ثم عن عرفطة

و هذا يقتضي جواز الحج عن الأموات و الأحياء أيضا بالنيابة إذا كانوا عاجزين عن الوصول لكن قياس القراءة على الحج مشكل لأن الحج فيه عمل بدني و عمل قلبي و عمل قولي و عمل مالي و القراءة هي مجرد عمل قولي و عمل قلبي و ليس فيها شيء من عمل بقية البدن و لا شيء من المال فلذلك قياسها قياس مع وجود الفارق فالراحج عدم وصولها
body_en:
What is known among us as al-tawfiyah for the dead — that is, reciting Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ eleven times on the night before Friday and sending its reward to the dead: does it reach them? And is it established in the sunnah or not?

This has not come down in the sunnah from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace. It is well known that the good is what the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, brought from God, and that whatever he did not bring has no good in it. Reciting the Qur'an and making a gift of its reward to the dead is a point of disagreement among the scholars. The position of Malik and al-Shafi'i is that it does not reach them. What is strange is that the people of this country are Malikis, and yet we find this custom widespread among them, while Malik's position is that it does not reach. Malik's position is that the recitation does not reach the dead, and that what does reach them is supplication and voluntary charity (ṣadaqah). Mawlud, may God have mercy on him, said: *The reward of food and of supplication, if they are given on the dead man's behalf — there is no disagreement that the two reach him.*

Even so, the position of Abu Hanifah and Ibn Hanbal is that reciting the Qur'an and making a gift of its reward to the deceased does reach him, if the gift precedes the recitation, by analogical reasoning (qiyās) from charity and supplication. This is what they call al-talḥīq, namely that a person says, before he recites: 'O God, make the reward of what I am about to recite and the blessing of what I am about to recite a gift from me, sent down, and a mercy from You, arriving, to so-and-so' — and he names him. This then constitutes a gift of that act to him.

The Hanbalis and the Hanafis drew this analogy from hajj and the lesser pilgrimage (ʿumrah), for the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, permitted hajj and ʿumrah on behalf of the dead. Al-Bukhari recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, may God be pleased with him, that a man of the Ansar came to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and said: 'My mother has died and did not perform hajj; shall I perform hajj on her behalf?' He said: 'Perform hajj on behalf of your mother.' In another narration: 'Perform hajj on behalf of your mother, and perform ʿumrah' — and that narration is Abu Dawud's, in the Sunan. Likewise in the hadith of the woman of Khathʿam, that she said: 'O Messenger of God, God's obligation of hajj has come upon my father as a very old man who cannot hold himself up on the mount; shall I perform hajj on his behalf?' He said: 'Tell me: if your father owed a debt, would you not have paid it?' She said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then discharge what is owed by him, for God's debt has the better right to be discharged.' And the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, heard a man saying: 'Here I am, O God, on behalf of Shubrumah.' He said: 'Have you performed hajj for yourself?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'Then perform hajj for yourself, and then for Shubrumah.' And he heard another saying: 'Here I am, O God, on behalf of ʿArfaṭah.' He said: 'Have you performed hajj for yourself?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'Then perform hajj for yourself, and then for ʿArfaṭah.'

This entails the permissibility of performing hajj on behalf of the dead, and on behalf of the living as well, by proxy, when they are unable to make the journey. But the analogy of recitation to hajj is problematic, because hajj contains bodily action, action of the heart, verbal action and financial action, whereas recitation is merely verbal action and action of the heart: there is nothing in it of the action of the rest of the body, and nothing of wealth. Its analogy is therefore an analogy drawn where a relevant difference is present. So the stronger view is that it does not reach them.

flags.context: ما يعرف عندنا بالتوفية للأموات أي قراءة سورة الإخلاص إحدى عشرة مرة ليلة الجمعة و إرسال ثوابها للأموات
options: al-tawfiyah — the local name for reciting Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ eleven times on the night before Friday and dedicating the reward to the dead
the 'discharging' (al-tawfiyah) — a reward-dedication rite performed for the dead
flags.note: Mauritanian regional term, glossed by the questioner himself ('what is known among us as…'). The English keeps the Arabic term because there is no settled English name for the practice. The Sheikh's office should confirm whether al-tawfiyah names this specific eleven-fold recitation or a wider family of rites.

flags.context: و هذا الذي يسمى بالتلحيق عندهم و هو أن يقول الإنسان قبل قراءته اللهم اجعل ثواب ما سأقرأ
options: al-talḥīq — dedicating the reward in advance of the recitation
flags.note: A Hanafi/Hanbali term of art reported here by the Sheikh, not his own usage ('what they call'). The attribution must remain visible in any rendering.

flags.context: و قد قال مولود رحمه الله: أجر الطعام و الدعا إن بذلا للميت لا خلاف في أن يصلا
options: Mawlud — a Mauritanian author of didactic verse, cited by first name only
Muhammad Mawlud al-Yaqubi al-Shinqiti, the Mauritanian versifier
flags.note: The Sheikh cites the poet by a single name, as is normal in the Shinqiti tradition where the naẓm is common knowledge. The English does not supply an identification; the Sheikh's office should confirm which Mawlud and which naẓm the line comes from before any note is added for readers.

translator_notes: Qur'anic and hadith renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic.
The single line of verse quoted from Mawlud is rendered as prose in italics per house style; no attempt has been made at rhymed English. The Arabic should be displayed alongside it.

Three spelling slips in the source have been preserved verbatim in body_ar and not carried into the English: القرآءة for القراءة, الدعا for الدعاء (inside the line of verse, where it may be metrical licence), and فالراحج for فالراجح in the closing sentence. The last of these is the word that carries the Sheikh's own conclusion, so it should be confirmed against another copy before publication.

The clause 'و مذهب مالك أنه لا يصل مذهب مالك أن القرآءة لا تصل الأموات' repeats itself in the source. The repetition has been kept in the Arabic and rendered once as a restatement in the English, which is how it reads.
The Sheikh gives al-Bukhari for the hadith of Anas and Abu Dawud's Sunan for the second narration, and gives no grading for the remaining reports. No grading has been supplied.
